sources.title: LGBT rights in Australia – Wikipedia
sources.claim: The article's territory notes are directly on point for the external territories: Norfolk Island has been incorporated into NSW legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016, and Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands — the Australian Indian Ocean Territories — are jurisdictions where WA laws apply. The page also records that 'X' sex-descriptor availability and anti-discrimination protection on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the states and territories with concurrent federal protection, and that same-sex adult private sexual conduct has been legal nationally since the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994. As the national-framework document for dependent territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, it supports this record's finding that visitors to Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Jervis Bay territory stand under the national/NSW/WA framework with no territory-specific SOGIE provision or divergence documented.

sources.title: Sex Discrimination Act 1984 – Wikipedia
sources.claim: The article records that the Commonwealth Sex Discrimination Act 1984 was amended by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013, so that discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status is prohibited — alongside sex, marital or relationship status, pregnancy and breastfeeding — across areas of public life including work, accommodation, education and the provision of goods and services. As a Commonwealth statute applying throughout Australia, including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law, this is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor on Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands or Jervis Bay territory stands under, confirming the national layer this record identifies with no locally diverging provision on the record.

records.name: Roraima
records.current_summary:
The national framework applies in Roraima with no documented state-level deviation: protections come from the federal supreme court — name and gender-marker change without surgery or court order, and the 2019 ruling equating anti-LGBT crimes with racism — rather than a comprehensive statute, and non-binary birth-certificate recognition is handled case-by-case state by state.

The country carries the world's highest absolute toll of killings of trans people, concentrated away from the capitals, and observers stress that protections are uneven in practice, thinning in the interior. The earlier specific claims for Roraima — no killings recorded for 2024, lowest national band for 2025 — lack a citation in this region's audited sources and are treated as unconfirmed; in so small a state a single case would dominate the statistics in any year, and official counts under-record.

For a visitor the picture is the national one with interior attenuation: rights on paper, thin services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility mechanism on record either.
records.current_localsOnly: Birth-certificate rectification for trans and non-binary people in Roraima runs through free judicial action (2025), not a state administrative channel.

sources.claim: Country-framework page (revised through 2026): same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report, last updated 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, updated April 2026): Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper - same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia/transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice: major cities (Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Florianopolis) are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

A current-status check confirms the federal framework (marriage equality since 2013, no criminalisation, nationwide document rectification) unchanged. No state-level hostility mechanism is on record.
